pair_preferences.rationale: Both fail true literal-path safety because neither quotes paths. Second narrowly wins for clearer separation and test -f.
Second is clearly better because it at least quotes paths containing spaces. Double quotes still do not safely handle every possible shell character, though.
All four debugging outputs produced the identical correct patch. Second explains the concrete leakage sequence better in repetition 1.
All four debugging outputs produced the identical correct patch. First explains why normalization was insufficient better in repetition 2.

First has stronger resolved-path layout validation, reports the backup during preflight, and restores exactly. This is close because its shallow file comparison and reusable backup directory are weaknesses.

Second recursively checks nested content. First only compares the top level, so it could still overwrite a hand-edited nested file without recognizing the conflict. Second unfortunately fails to reject nested source/destination layouts.
Both produce the same supplied-case result and share essentially the same limitations: hardcoded snapshot filenames, no applicability filtering, and omission of completed runs from outcome_counts.

Second decisively wins. It filters for applicable advisories, chooses the newest one, preserves all statuses including completed, and always produces a classification. First hardcodes the signed snapshot and can return classification=None.

benchmark_limitation: The corrected runner executed tests successfully, but several clearly incomplete implementations still passed. The visible two-test suites are too weak to discriminate important edge cases, so this run cannot by itself establish that compiler v2 succeeds or fails.
